title: Enhancing Hallucination Detection through Noise Injection
claim: Sampling only at the output captures aleatoric uncertainty; also injecting noise at earlier stages captures epistemic uncertainty.
layout: 1 panel, bottom-to-top architecture stack, dashed arrows with side labels
description: A single vertical diagram of a Transformer architecture, read bottom to top. Pastel boxes are stacked from Input through Embeddings, then a dashed gray block labeled Nx containing Attention and Feed Forward with residual skip arrows. Above it come Linear, Softmax, and Output. On the left, two bold labels with dashed black arrows point into the stack. 'Aleatoric: Temperature Sampling at Prediction Stage' points at the Softmax layer. 'Epistemic: Noise Injection at Earlier Stages' points into the Nx block. An orange italic 'Transformer Architecture' label sits at the bottom left. The eye goes first to the large black labels and arrows, then to the colored layer boxes.
caption: Inference-time hallucination detection typically relies solely on temperature-based sampling at the prediction layer, capturing mainly aleatoric uncertainty [ref]. We introduce noise injection to perturb intermediate representations. By combining noise injection with prediction layer sampling, our sampling approach captures both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating plausible yet incorrect responses, known as hallucinations. Effectively detecting hallucinations is therefore crucial for the safe deployment of LLMs. Recent research has linked hallucinations to model uncertainty, suggesting that hallucinations can be detected by measuring dispersion over answer distributions obtained from multiple samples drawn from a model. While drawing from the distribution over tokens defined by the model is a natural way to obtain samples, in this work, we argue that it is suboptimal for the purpose of detecting hallucinations. We show that detection can be improved significantly by taking into account model uncertainty in the Bayesian sense. To this end, we propose a very simple, training-free approach based on perturbing an appropriate subset of model parameters, or equivalently hidden unit activations, during sampling. We demonstrate that our approach significantly improves inference-time hallucination detection over standard sampling across diverse datasets, model architectures, and uncertainty metrics.
